language-development-s2.title: Babies hearing sounds from other languages

study.introduction: Janet Werker and Richard Tees asked whether babies raised hearing English can tell apart speech sounds that English does not use but Hindi and a First Nations language (Nthlakampx) do.
study.participants: Infants from English-speaking homes in Canada, tested at 6 to 8, 8 to 10 and 10 to 12 months, some of them followed across these ages. Infants learning Hindi or Nthlakampx were also tested.
study.method: Each baby heard one speech sound repeated, then a switch to a similar sound. Babies were trained to turn their heads toward a toy display when they heard the sound change; a head turn right after a switch counted as noticing the difference.
study.results: Most 6- to 8-month-olds from English-speaking homes noticed the non-English sound differences. By 10 to 12 months, few did. Babies learning Hindi or Nthlakampx still noticed the differences in their own languages at 10 to 12 months.
study.discussion: Babies start able to hear sound differences from many languages and, by their first birthday, tune in to the sounds of the language around them.

language-development-s3.title: Words heard in a short visit
language-development-s3.text: A researcher recorded how many different words each of five 18-month-olds said during a 30-minute home visit.

table.caption: Different words spoken in 30 minutes (invented data for practice)

items.q: A 6-month-old says "ba-ba-ba, da-da-da" while playing alone. Which milestone in the figure is this?
options: Babbling
Cooing
The one-word stage
Telegraphic speech

why.correct: Babbling begins around 6 months and gradually takes on the sounds of the home language.
options: Right: repeated consonant-vowel syllables, made in play, are babbling.
Cooing is vowel-like sounds such as "ooh," which come earlier, around 2 months.
Repeating syllables in play is not using a word to mean something.
Telegraphic speech combines two or more words.

items.q: A 13-month-old points at the door and says "Out!" meaning "I want to go outside." Which stage does this show?
options: Telegraphic speech
Babbling
Overgeneralization
The one-word stage

why.correct: Around the first birthday, children use single words that carry a sentence of meaning.
options: Telegraphic speech uses two or more words, such as "Go out."
Babbling is syllables made in play, without meaning.
Overgeneralization is applying a grammar rule where it does not fit.
Right: a single word stands for a whole idea.

items.q: A 2-year-old says "Daddy go car." Which stage is this, and what does it show?
options: Babbling: sounds without meaning
Cooing: vowel-like sounds
Telegraphic speech: key words in order
The one-word stage: one word stands for a whole idea

why.correct: Telegraphic speech follows the word order (syntax) of the language even though it leaves out small words.
options: Each word has a clear meaning.
Cooing comes in the first months and has no words.
Right: like a telegram, it keeps content words in order and drops "is," "in" and "the."
The child uses three words.

items.q: Near the end of the timeline, a child says "I goed outside" and "I saw two mouses." What do these errors show?
options: Babbling: sounds without meaning
Overgeneralization of grammar rules
That the child is copying adults’ words exactly
Telegraphic speech: leaving out small words

why.correct: These errors are a good sign: the child has learned a rule and is using it.
options: The words have clear meanings.
Right: the child applies the "-ed" and "-s" rules to irregular words.
Adults do not say "goed," so the child is using a rule, not copying.
Nothing is left out; a rule is applied too widely.

items.q: Werker and Tees found that 6- to 8-month-olds from English-speaking homes could hear sound differences from Hindi. Which unit of language were the babies telling apart?
options: Phonemes, the smallest units of sound
Morphemes, the smallest units of meaning
Syntax, the rules for word order
Semantics, the rules for meaning

why.correct: A phoneme is a basic speech sound; languages use different sets of phonemes.
options: Right: the babies heard differences between speech sounds.
The sounds were not words or word parts with meaning.
No words were put in order.
The task was about sounds, not meaning.

items.q: Which statement best summarizes the results?
options: Older babies were better at noticing speech sound differences in general
Babies learning Hindi lost the ability to hear Hindi sounds
Babies could not tell any sounds apart until 10 months
By age 1, babies tuned in to their own language’s sounds

why.correct: Early hearing is broad; experience narrows it toward the home language.
options: English-learning babies got worse at the non-English differences as they got older.
They still noticed the differences in their own language.
Most 6- to 8-month-olds noticed the differences.
Right: English-learning babies stopped noticing non-English differences by 10 to 12 months, while babies learning Hindi kept noticing theirs.

items.q: Which idea from physical development do these results support?
options: Imprinting, the bond young geese form with a moving object
Menarche, the first menstrual period
A sensitive period for hearing speech sounds
Teratogens, which harm development before birth

why.correct: Early experience has its strongest effect during a sensitive period; adults can still learn new sounds with practice, though with more effort.
options: Imprinting is a social bond, not speech perception.
That is a milestone of puberty.
Right: hearing the home language in the first year narrows which sound differences babies notice.
Nothing harmful is involved.

items.q: What is the mean number of different words the five children said?

mistakes.why: That is the total. Divide by the number of children, 5.
That is the range (19 minus 4). The mean is the total divided by 5.

items.q: What is the range of the number of different words?

mistakes.why: That is the highest value. Subtract the lowest, 4.
You added the highest and lowest. The range is the difference.

items.q: What does the spread of these numbers suggest about language development at 18 months?
options: Child T has a language disorder
Each child should be saying about 10 words
The children are in the cooing stage
Healthy toddlers vary widely in word use

why.correct: Milestones come in a similar order, but vocabulary size varies a great deal between healthy children.
options: One high count in one visit does not show a disorder, and T is ahead.
The mean describes the group, not a target for each child.
Cooing has no words; all five children used words.
Right: a range of 15 words in one visit is typical variation at this age.

items.q: The word "unhappiness" can be split into "un," "happy" and "ness," each carrying meaning. What are these parts?
options: Syntax rules
Babbling sounds
Morphemes
Phonemes

why.correct: Phonemes build morphemes; morphemes build words.
options: Syntax is about word order in sentences.
Babbling is an infant stage of making syllables.
Right: a morpheme is the smallest unit that carries meaning.
Phonemes are sounds; "un" has two of them but one meaning.

items.q: "The dog bit the man" and "The man bit the dog" use the same words but mean different things. Which part of grammar explains this?
options: Cooing, an early infant sound
Syntax, the rules for word order
Phonemes, the smallest sound units
Morphemes, the smallest units of meaning

why.correct: Grammar includes semantics (meaning) and syntax (order); here the order carries the meaning.
options: Cooing is a stage of infancy.
Right: changing the order changed who did what.
The sounds are the same; the order differs.
Both sentences have the same morphemes.

items.q: A 4-year-old says, "The zorp is snoozling on the blicket," a sentence nobody has ever said to her. What does this show about language?
options: Generativity: rules create new sentences
Telegraphic speech: leaving out small words
That she is copying a sentence she heard on TV
The one-word stage

why.correct: Generativity is the ability to produce and understand an unlimited number of new sentences.
options: Right: she combined words with grammar rules to make a sentence she never heard.
Her sentence includes "is," "on" and "the."
No one has said it to her.
She used a full sentence.

items.q: A child knows "hot" means something that burns and learns that "cool" can also mean "great." Which aspect of language is she learning?
options: Syntax, the rules for word order
Phonemes, the smallest speech sounds
Babbling, an early infant stage
Semantics, the rules of meaning

why.correct: Semantics covers meaning, including multiple meanings of a word.
options: Word order is not what she is learning here.
The sounds are unchanged; the meaning is new.
She is long past babbling.
Right: semantics is about what words and sentences mean.

items.q: Put these stages of early language in the order they usually appear.
options: Cooing ("ooh," "aah")
Babbling ("ba-ba-ba")
One-word stage ("Doggy!")
Telegraphic speech ("Want juice.")

why.correct: Cooing (about 2 months), babbling (about 6 months), one word (about 12 months), telegraphic speech (about 18 to 24 months).
